pillar: How to Prepare for Major Cancer Surgery: Prehabilitation and Nutrition

items.q: What is prehabilitation before cancer surgery?
items.a: Prehabilitation is a structured programme of exercise, nutrition and stress support that you follow in the weeks before an operation to make your body stronger for it. It usually combines walking or light resistance training, extra protein, breathing exercises, and help with anxiety or smoking. Studies suggest patients who prehabilitate often recover faster and spend fewer days in hospital. Your surgical team can advise what is realistic in your timeline.

items.q: How long before surgery should I start preparing?
items.a: Two to four weeks is the usual window, and even seven to ten days can help. Most prehabilitation research uses about four weeks of exercise and nutrition support before major abdominal or chest surgery. If your operation is sooner, focus on protein intake, daily walking and breathing exercises rather than trying to do everything at once. Surgery should rarely be delayed for prehabilitation unless your team specifically recommends it.

items.q: How much protein do I need before surgery?
items.a: Most surgical nutrition guidelines suggest roughly 1.2 to 1.5 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight each day before major cancer surgery. For a 60 kg person that is about 72 to 90 grams daily, spread across meals such as eggs, dairy, lentils, fish, chicken or paneer. Protein helps protect muscle and supports wound healing. Anyone with kidney disease should confirm their target with a doctor or dietitian first.

items.q: What if I have already lost weight and cannot eat much?
items.a: Unintended weight loss before cancer surgery is common, and it needs attention rather than waiting. Tell your team quickly, because they can arrange oral nutrition supplements, small frequent high-calorie meals, or medication for nausea and taste changes. Losing more than five percent of your body weight in six months can raise the risk of complications. In some cases feeding through a tube is started before surgery to rebuild reserves.

items.q: Will exercise before surgery actually make a difference?
items.a:
In many cases, yes. Trials in lung, bowel and abdominal cancer surgery show that patients who improve their fitness beforehand often have fewer chest infections and shorter hospital stays. The usual target is about 20 to 30 minutes of moderate activity most days, plus simple resistance work for the legs and arms.

Start at whatever level you can manage, and stop if you feel chest pain or severe breathlessness.

items.q: Should I stop smoking or drinking before my operation?
items.a: Yes, and the sooner the better. Stopping smoking at least four weeks before surgery can meaningfully lower the risk of wound and lung complications, and four weeks without alcohol can improve bleeding and immune function. Even a few days without smoking helps oxygen reach healing tissue. Ask your team about nicotine replacement or withdrawal support, because quitting under the stress of a cancer diagnosis is genuinely hard.

items.q: What breathing exercises help before chest or abdominal surgery?
items.a: Inspiratory muscle training, usually done with a small handheld device, strengthens the muscles you breathe with and can reduce the chance of pneumonia after surgery. A typical plan is about 15 minutes a day for two to four weeks. Simple deep breathing and coughing practice also helps, especially if you will have a chest or upper abdominal incision. A physiotherapist can set the resistance level correctly for you.

items.q: Can I prehabilitate if I am having chemotherapy first?
items.a: Yes. Many patients receiving chemotherapy or chemoradiation before surgery prehabilitate at the same time, doing lighter exercise on the days they feel worst. The aim shifts towards protecting muscle and weight rather than building peak fitness. Blood counts, fatigue and nerve symptoms may change what is safe, so activity often needs adjusting week to week. Your oncologist and physiotherapist can agree a plan that fits your treatment cycles.

items.q: How do I prepare if I am travelling to India or China for surgery?
items.a: Start prehabilitation at home before you fly, because the weeks spent arranging visas, funds and appointments are useful training time. Carry recent blood tests, imaging and a record of your weight so the receiving team can assess your nutritional status on arrival. Plan for jet lag, food you can actually eat, and a companion to help. CancerFax can often share your records with the hospital ahead of travel.

items.q: What should I ask my surgical team before the operation?
items.a: Ask what your specific complication risks are, whether a dietitian or prehabilitation referral is available, how long recovery usually takes for this operation, and what would make them postpone it. Also ask what fitness or nutrition target they want you to reach. Bring your questions written down and a family member to take notes. A second opinion is reasonable, and CancerFax may be able to help arrange one.
